What Drives Household Food Spending? A Regression Analysis

Parnika Raina

2026-01-19

About This Project

An individual applied regression project using real household expenditure data, working from a business question through data cleaning, modelling, and interpretation to reach a conclusion.

Business Problem

Understanding what drives a household’s weekly food spending is useful for anyone trying to model or predict household budgets. This analysis looks at household characteristics and spending patterns, and specifically asks whether the relationship between alcohol spending and food spending changes depending on how much debt a household carries. If it does, debt level would be an important segmentation factor; if it doesn’t, one model can be used across debt levels without splitting the population up.

Data Dictionary

This data covers weekly household expenditure in England. The variables are described below.

Variable Description
Kids Number of kids in the household
HouseholdSize Number of members living in the household
Sex The sex of the survey respondent (male/female)
Vehicles Number of vehicles owned by the household
Food Average amount spent on food per week
Housing Average amount spent on accommodation per week
Alcohol Average weekly spend on alcohol
Debt Average weekly spend on debt repayments
income_category The household’s income level (Low/Medium/High)

A few variables have a handful of missing values, there are no duplicate households, and the figures all look realistic - so filtering out the missing values is the only cleaning needed before moving on.

Filtering the data

cat("Rows before filtering:", nrow(Household_data), "\n\n")
## Rows before filtering: 4097
# Removing the missing data in key variables
household_filtered <- Household_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Food),           
         !is.na(Alcohol),        
         !is.na(Debt),
         !is.na(Vehicles),
         !is.na(Kids), 
         !is.na(Housing),
         !is.na(HouseholdSize), 
         !is.na(Sex),
         !is.na(income_category)) 
# Converting categorical variables to factors

household_filtered <- household_filtered %>%
  mutate(
    Sex = factor(Sex),
    income_category = factor(income_category, 
                            levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"), 
                            ordered = FALSE)
  )

cat("Rows after filtering:", nrow(household_filtered), "\n")
## Rows after filtering: 4083
cat("Percentage of data retained:", 
    round(100 * nrow(household_filtered) / nrow(Household_data), 1), "%\n\n")
## Percentage of data retained: 99.7 %
summary(household_filtered)

Almost every household was retained after filtering, so very little information was lost and the data is still representative. Categorical variables were converted to factors before modelling, so R treats them as groups rather than as numbers.

Demonstrating the Distribution of the Relevant Variables

Food Distribution

  ggplot(household_filtered, aes(x = Food)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "pink", colour = "black" ) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Weekly Food Expenditure",
        x = "Food Expenditure (£/week)", y = "Number of Households") +
  theme_minimal()

Most households spend between £50 and £60 a week on food, and spending is fairly balanced around that middle range rather than skewed by a few very high or very low spenders. That makes a linear regression model a reasonable choice here.

Debt Distribution

  ggplot(household_filtered, aes(x = Debt)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black") +
  labs( title = "Distribution of weekly debt payments", x = "Debt Payments (£/week)", y = "Number of Households") +
  theme_minimal()

Debt payments are less evenly spread - most households pay between £40 and £70 a week, with fewer at the very low or very high end. Because debt isn’t evenly distributed, it makes sense to check whether households at different debt levels show a different relationship between alcohol and food spending.

Alcohol Distribution

  ggplot(household_filtered, aes(x = Alcohol)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "orange", colour = "black") +
  labs( title =  "Distribution of Weekly Alcohol Expenditure", x = "Alcohol Expenditure (£/week)", y = "Number of Households") +
  theme_minimal()

The average household spends between £15 and £20 a week on alcohol, with relatively few spending a lot more or a lot less.

Demonstrating the Relationships of the Relevant Variables

Food vs Housing

ggplot(household_filtered, aes(x = Housing, y = Food)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "orange") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red") +
  labs( title= "Food Expenditure vs Housing Costs", x = "Housing (£/week)", y = "Food (£/week)")
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Food spending tends to rise a little as housing costs rise, though the relationship is fairly loose - useful as a control variable in a model, but not a strong predictor of food spending on its own.

Alcohol vs Food

ggplot(household_filtered, aes(x = Alcohol, y = Food, colour = income_category)) + 
geom_point(alpha = 0.25) +
geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
theme_minimal() +
labs(title = "Alcohol vs Food by Income category",
    x = "Weekly Alcohol spend (£)", y = "Weekly food spend (£)",
    colour = "Income category")
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Across all income groups, food spending rises slightly as alcohol spending rises, and the pattern looks much the same whether a household is on a low, medium, or high income.

Food vs Debt

ggplot(household_filtered, aes(x = Debt, y = Food)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "purple") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red") +
  labs( title = "Food vs Debt Payments", x = "Debt (£/week)", y = "Food (£/week)")
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Debt on its own has only a weak relationship with food spending, which suggests food spending isn’t something debt alone can explain - a good reason to build a model that accounts for several household factors at once rather than looking at any one variable in isolation.

Food vs Alcohol Across Debt Bands

household_filtered %>%
  mutate(
    DebtBand = cut(
      Debt,
      breaks = quantile(Debt, probs = c(0, 0.33, 0.66, 1), na.rm = TRUE),
      labels = c("Low debt", "Medium debt", "High debt"),
      include.lowest = TRUE
    )
  ) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    aes(Alcohol, Food),
    alpha = 0.2,
    colour = "pink"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(Alcohol, Food),
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "red"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ DebtBand) +
  labs(
    title = "Food vs Alcohol Across Debt Bands",
    x = "Weekly Alcohol Spend (£)",
    y = "Weekly Food Spend (£)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Households at low, medium, and high debt levels all show a similar pattern: food spending rises somewhat as alcohol spending rises. At a glance, debt doesn’t look like it’s changing that relationship - worth checking formally with a model.

Model 1

m.food <- lm(Food ~ HouseholdSize + Sex + Vehicles + Housing + Kids +
               Alcohol + Debt + income_category, data = household_filtered)

summary(m.food)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = Food ~ HouseholdSize + Sex + Vehicles + Housing + 
##     Kids + Alcohol + Debt + income_category, data = household_filtered)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -42.300  -8.124  -0.090   8.081  39.699 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                        Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)           23.472590   1.688695  13.900  < 2e-16 ***
## HouseholdSize          0.175645   0.291747   0.602   0.5472    
## Sexmale               -0.083423   0.405226  -0.206   0.8369    
## Vehicles               0.360337   0.216622   1.663   0.0963 .  
## Housing                0.091439   0.003485  26.241  < 2e-16 ***
## Kids                  -0.412563   0.354191  -1.165   0.2442    
## Alcohol                0.388444   0.062415   6.224 5.35e-10 ***
## Debt                  -0.049175   0.009718  -5.060 4.38e-07 ***
## income_categoryMedium  0.928248   0.477733   1.943   0.0521 .  
## income_categoryHigh    0.392923   0.749619   0.524   0.6002    
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 11.91 on 4073 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.1536, Adjusted R-squared:  0.1517 
## F-statistic:  82.1 on 9 and 4073 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
cbind(coef(m.food), confint(m.food))
##                                          2.5 %      97.5 %
## (Intercept)           23.47258986 20.161823787 26.78335593
## HouseholdSize          0.17564548 -0.396338881  0.74762984
## Sexmale               -0.08342262 -0.877887408  0.71104218
## Vehicles               0.36033683 -0.064361166  0.78503482
## Housing                0.09143859  0.084606809  0.09827037
## Kids                  -0.41256305 -1.106971175  0.28184507
## Alcohol                0.38844391  0.266075449  0.51081238
## Debt                  -0.04917521 -0.068228709 -0.03012171
## income_categoryMedium  0.92824782 -0.008370389  1.86486603
## income_categoryHigh    0.39292268 -1.076740484  1.86258585

This model looks at weekly food spending against household characteristics and other spending, all together. It’s statistically significant overall, meaning these variables jointly help explain food spending.

The model explains about 15% of the variation in food spending - a modest amount, but reasonable for household survey data where a lot of what drives someone’s spending simply isn’t captured here.

Housing and alcohol spending are the strongest predictors: households that spend more on either tend to spend more on food too, while higher debt is linked to slightly lower food spending. Household size, number of children, sex, and income category don’t show a significant effect once spending patterns are accounted for, and vehicle ownership’s relationship is weak and unclear.

Model 2

m.interaction <- lm(
  Food ~ HouseholdSize + Kids + Vehicles + Housing +
    income_category + Sex + Alcohol * Debt,
  data = household_filtered
)

summary(m.interaction)

## lm(formula = Food ~ HouseholdSize + Kids + Vehicles + Housing +

## Vehicles               0.358828   0.216663   1.656   0.0978 .

confint(m.interaction)
##                              2.5 %       97.5 %
## (Intercept)           14.949131847 28.881893918
## HouseholdSize         -0.396836589  0.747243120
## Kids                  -1.108177360  0.280795586
## Vehicles              -0.065950708  0.783606795
## Housing                0.084572459  0.098239679
## income_categoryMedium -0.007365523  1.866064042
## income_categoryHigh   -1.071858860  1.868019463
## Sexmale               -0.880839790  0.708389751
## Alcohol                0.096330125  0.865912496
## Debt                  -0.128599782  0.083169216
## Alcohol:Debt          -0.007646147  0.004548258

This model tests directly whether the relationship between alcohol and food spending changes at different debt levels, by adding an alcohol-by-debt interaction term. It’s statistically significant overall.

Alcohol spending still has a positive relationship with food spending, and housing remains the strongest predictor. But the interaction between alcohol and debt itself isn’t statistically significant - meaning debt doesn’t meaningfully change how alcohol relates to food spending. As before, household size, number of children, sex, and income category don’t show a significant effect once spending is accounted for.

Anova Test

anova(m.food, m.interaction)
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Model 1: Food ~ HouseholdSize + Sex + Vehicles + Housing + Kids + Alcohol + 
##     Debt + income_category
## Model 2: Food ~ HouseholdSize + Kids + Vehicles + Housing + income_category + 
##     Sex + Alcohol * Debt
##   Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F Pr(>F)
## 1   4073 578186                           
## 2   4072 578150  1    35.221 0.2481 0.6185

Adding the alcohol-debt interaction doesn’t improve the model in a statistically meaningful way. This confirms the simpler model without the interaction is enough: alcohol’s relationship with food spending doesn’t really depend on a household’s debt level.

Emmeans

emmeans(
  m.interaction,
  specs = ~ Alcohol | Debt,
  at = list(
    Alcohol = c(10, 15, 20),
    Debt = quantile(household_filtered$Debt, c(.25,.50,.75))
  )
)
## Debt = 49.5:
##  Alcohol emmean    SE   df lower.CL upper.CL
##       10   55.0 0.537 4072     53.9     56.0
##       15   57.0 0.288 4072     56.4     57.6
##       20   59.0 0.353 4072     58.3     59.7
## 
## Debt = 59.9:
##  Alcohol emmean    SE   df lower.CL upper.CL
##       10   54.6 0.498 4072     53.6     55.6
##       15   56.5 0.272 4072     56.0     57.1
##       20   58.5 0.307 4072     57.9     59.1
## 
## Debt = 70.8:
##  Alcohol emmean    SE   df lower.CL upper.CL
##       10   54.2 0.584 4072     53.0     55.3
##       15   56.0 0.310 4072     55.4     56.6
##       20   57.9 0.322 4072     57.2     58.5
## 
## Results are averaged over the levels of: income_category, Sex 
## Confidence level used: 0.95

Predicted food spending rises as alcohol spending rises, at every debt level. The size of that increase is similar whether debt is low, medium, or high - consistent with the ANOVA result above, confirming debt doesn’t meaningfully change the alcohol-food relationship, even though households with higher debt do tend to spend a little less on food overall.

Conclusion

Food spending rises as alcohol spending rises, and this relationship holds fairly consistently across low, medium, and high debt households - the interaction between alcohol and debt was not statistically significant. Housing and alcohol spending are the two strongest predictors of food spending overall, while household size, number of children, sex, and income category don’t add much once spending patterns are accounted for. For anyone modelling household food spending, this suggests debt level doesn’t need to be treated as a special segmentation factor for the alcohol relationship specifically, though it’s still a useful control variable in its own right.
